spoken: Swift-footed Achilles, the greatest of the Greek heroes, is racing a tortoise. And the tortoise has a head start.
That hardly seems fair. On the tortoise, I mean.
Ah, but listen. Each time Achilles reaches the spot where the tortoise was, it has crept a little further on.
So, says an argument nearly 2,500 years old, he can never catch it.
Which is plainly wrong. Of course he catches it.
Sure. But saying exactly what's wrong with the argument took more than 2,000 years, and some philosophers say it still isn't settled.
This is Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise.
Zeno was born around 490 BC in Ellia, a Greek city on the west coast of southern Italy.
And he was a student and friend of an older philosopher, Parmenides.
Parmenides taught that reality is one unchanging whole, and that change and motion are illusions.
Illusions? Motion itself?
Motion itself. You can imagine how that went down.
Critics found it absurd. So Zeno turned the tables, showing that their views, followed through, led to worse absurdities.
That style of argument is called reductio ad absurdum, and Aristotle called Zeno the inventor of dialectic.
Sadly, Zeno's book is lost. Fewer than two hundred of his own words survive.
So we know his arguments from others, such as Plato, Aristotle, and Simplishius, writing a thousand years later.
Plato even has the two visit Athens to meet a young Socrates, though he probably invented that meeting.
A good scene, then, but probably not history.
The most famous argument is a race. Aristotle gives it in his Physics, like this.
In a race, the quickest runner can never overtake the slowest, since the pursuer must first reach the point whence the pursued started,
so that the slower must always hold a lead.
Hang on. There's no tortoise in that, just the slowest runner.
Right. The tortoise comes from later retellings.
Then let's race. Achilles runs ten metres a second, and the tortoise one metre a second.
And the tortoise starts 100 metres ahead.
In stage one, Achilles runs those hundred metres, which takes him ten seconds.
But in those 10 seconds, the tortoise has crawled 10 metres further.
In stage two, he covers those ten metres in one second, and the tortoise crawls another metre.
Stage three leaves a gap of 10 centimetres, and stage four leaves just 1 centimetre.
And each time we zoom in ten times, the picture looks exactly the same.
Each gap is a tenth of the one before. It shrinks forever, but it never reaches zero.
So there's always one more stage, and Zeno concludes that Achilles never catches up.
So how far does Achilles actually run before he draws level? Let's add up the stages.
It's a hundred metres, plus ten, plus one, plus a tenth, plus a hundredth, and so on.
The running totals are 100, then 110, then 111, then 111.1, then 111.11.
They close in on one hundred and eleven and one ninth metres, with the ones repeating forever.
So the total doesn't run away to infinity.
No. And the times add up the same way, to eleven and one ninth seconds.
That's infinitely many stages, but they add up to a finite distance, and a finite time.
Plot distance against time, and each runner is a straight line. They cross at eleven point one seconds, and a hundred and eleven point one metres.
And Zeno's stages are a staircase closing in on that crossing, every one of them before it.
So where on the staircase does he catch up?
Nowhere. The moment he catches up isn't one of the stages. It comes just after all of them.
People often say Zeno thought infinitely many pieces must add up to something infinite.
But no ancient source has him discussing an infinite sum at all.
In Simplishius's report, his worry is that it is impossible to traverse an infinite number of things in a finite time.
So the puzzle isn't the total. It's how anyone can finish infinitely many steps, with no last one.
And that's a much harder question.
Zeno's dichotomy makes the same point, without any tortoise.
In Aristotle's words, that which is in locomotion must arrive at the half-way stage before it arrives at the goal.
So to run a hundred metres, first run half of it. Then half of what's left, then half of that.
The running totals are one half, three quarters, seven eighths, fifteen sixteenths, creeping towards the whole.
After ten halvings, you've run all but one part in a thousand and twenty-four, and less than ten centimetres is left.
After 20, less than a tenth of a millimetre is left. But there's always a half still to run.
Like a to-do list that grows exactly as fast as you work through it.
And there's a nastier version. Before the half-way mark, you must reach the quarter mark, and before that, the eighth.
Then the run has no first step at all. So how does it ever begin?
Aristotle noted that the Achilles is much the same argument. In our race, the gaps shrink by tenths, not halves.
Zeno's arrow attacks motion from the other side, by cutting time into instants.
Take an arrow in flight, and freeze a single instant.
In that instant, it fills a space exactly its own size, so it isn't moving.
But the whole flight is made of instants like this one. So when does the arrow ever move?
That one is slippery.
Aristotle's reply was that time is not made of indivisible nows, any more than a line is made of points.
The modern answer treats speed at an instant as a limit.
Say it flies at 50 metres a second. In a tenth of a second, it goes 5 metres.
And in a hundredth, half a metre. Distance over time stays at fifty metres a second, however short the interval.
But in a single instant it goes nowhere, and zero divided by zero isn't a number at all.
So the speed at an instant is defined as that limit.
On this view, motion doesn't happen inside an instant. It is being in different places at different times.
It sounds almost too simple.
The last of the four, the stadium, has rows of equal blocks passing each other in opposite directions.
The front block of one row passes every oncoming block, but only half of the still ones.
And from this, Zeno concluded that half a given time is equal to double that time.
Half equals double? That can't be right.
The usual verdict is that he ignored relative speed, since the oncoming blocks approach twice as fast.
One famous reply to Zeno wasn't an argument at all.
Simplishius tells a story. When Diogenes the Cynic heard Zeno's arguments, he said nothing, stood up, and walked.
That kind of answer even has a Latin name, solvitur ambulando, which means it is solved by walking.
Honestly, it's tempting.
It is. But walking only shows that the conclusion is false. It doesn't show which step of the argument fails.
Aristotle noted that shorter distances take shorter times. But then the time, too, is made of infinitely many pieces.
So his deeper answer splits infinity in two.
An actual infinity would be a completed collection of infinitely many things, all there at once.
And a potential infinity is a process that can always go on, but is never completed.
A path, he said, holds infinitely many halves only potentially. They'd be actual only if the runner stopped at each one.
So a smooth run never has to tick the halves off one by one.
In his words, if the units are actual, it is not possible; if they are potential, it is possible.
And that answer satisfied nearly all scholars for about 1,500 years.
Meanwhile, mathematicians were learning to tame infinite sums.
In the third century BC, Archimedes found the area of a slice cut from a parabola.
He filled it with triangles, and each new row of triangles has a quarter of the area of the row before.
So the slice is the big triangle, times one, plus a quarter, plus a sixteenth, and so on.
And Archimedes showed that this comes to exactly four thirds of the big triangle.
An infinite sum with a tidy answer, long before calculus.
But infinite sums can be slippery. Take one, minus one, plus one, minus one, and so on.
Pair the terms one way and you get zero. Pair them another way and you get one.
Zero and one, from the same sum?
That's the trouble. In 1821, the French mathematician Augustin Louis Koh-shee insisted on strict tests of when a sum makes sense.
Its value is the number its running totals settle down to, if they settle at all.
Then a half, plus a quarter, plus an eighth, is exactly one, while one minus one plus one has no sum.
In eighteen sixty-one, Karl Weierstrass gave the definition of a limit in the precise form used today.
Pick any margin, however small. From some stage on, every running total stays within it.
For a margin of a millimetre, Achilles' totals stay inside it from stage six on. For a micrometre, it's from stage nine.
So 111.1 metres is the limit of Zeno's stages. Some historians, such as Carl Boyer, say calculus solves the paradox.
Case closed, then?
Not for everyone. The maths says where and when he draws level, but how does he finish infinitely many tasks?
Bertrand Russell argued that Achilles really does complete infinitely many tasks, in a finite time.
And in 1954, the philosopher James Thomson replied with a lamp.
Switch it on. After a minute, switch it off. After half a minute, on again, then off after a quarter.
Each wait is half the last, and the waits add up to exactly 2 minutes.
So at two minutes, is the lamp on or off?
Well, it has to be one or the other.
But it can't be on, because every time it went on, it was switched off again. And off fails for the same reason.
So Thomson concluded that a supertask, infinitely many tasks in a finite time, is impossible.
Its switch flips like the running totals of one minus one plus one, which never settle.
In 1962, Paul Benacerraf objected that the story fixes the lamp before 2 minutes, but says nothing about that moment itself.
So there's no contradiction, just a question the story leaves open.
Which is somehow satisfying and unsatisfying at the same time.
Philosophers still disagree about what counts as a task, and whether a supertask is possible.
And some theories of quantum gravity suggest that space and time may not divide endlessly at all.
As the philosopher Kevin Brown put it, it's probably foolhardy to think we've reached the end.
So, back to the race.
Achilles reaches the tortoise's start after ten seconds, and draws level after eleven point one seconds, at a hundred and eleven point one metres.
Before that moment come infinitely many of Zeno's stages, and every one of them fits inside those 11.1 seconds.
Zeno was wrong that motion is impossible. But he made us say what we mean by infinity, a sum, and an instant.
Not bad, for a puzzle about a tortoise.
Bertrand Russell wrote that Zeno's arguments have afforded grounds for almost all theories of space, time and infinity since.
Achilles wins the race. But Zeno's argument, it seems, is still running.
